newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thousands of ravers swamp Berlin for Love Parade.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of ravers swamp Berlin for Love Parade.

text.p: Hundreds of thousands of techno music fans flooded the streets of Berlin on Saturday, gearing up for the ninth annual Love Parade, a dance festival expected to draw one million people.

Overcrowded buses and cars with visitors from across Europe caused traffic jams across the country's motorways and up to two-hour delays at the city's main train station as young people made their way to the event.
Some launched an impromptu "rave" on Friday evening in front of the Zoologischer Garten station soon after stepping off the platforms.
"We had friends who were here last year and they said it was brilliant," said John White, 23, from Dublin. "There's just love in techno -- there's no hate."
Techno music is a mix of thundering beats and repetitive electronic bleats supplied by disc jockeys equipped with massive sound systems.
"The thing about techno is that because there is no text, you can just let your imagination go," said Martin Mueller, 19-year-old from Augsburg in southern Germany.
"All this ambience is more important than the music," said Alexia Cornel, a 27-year-old history student from Marseilles, France.

Cornel, decked out in a red and blue jester's hat, matching nail polish and red ski trousers, said she and her friends planned to sleep at the station or in a park if they could not find a room in a hostel.

Most accomodation has been booked for weeks with people coming from as far afield as South Africa, Australia and the United States. The Love Parade has become an essential stop on any backpacker's European tour.
Hundreds rested up for Saturday in the city's giant Tiergarten park, while three thousand others hijacked the posh Kurfuerstendamm shopping avenue for an all-night party.
Police were investigating numerous threats of violence by right- and left-wing extremists.

Berlin Interior Minister Joerg Schoenbohm received an anonymous letter thought to have been sent by neo-Nazis in which the author said three anti-tank mines would be laid along the parade route if the event was staged.
Anarchist punks had planned to hold their annual "Chaos Days" riot during the parade as a protest against the parade's commercialism, and some were dubbing their rival march a "Hate Parade".
The Love Parade has swelled in size since its modest first staging shortly before the Berlin Wall fell in 1989. It drew 750,000 revellers last year.

The street dancers gyrate down a six-km (four-mile) stretch of an eight-lane boulevard blocked off for the event, forming a giant "U" which bends a few hundred metres (yards) from the Brandenburg Gate.

Environmentalists tried to block the event this year by raising the spectre of mountains of garbage and human waste flooding the Tiergarten, but city officials, eager to see the massive revenues the parade rakes in, agreed to play hosts once again.
